title: Caste in your own life
hookLine: noticing caste thinking in yourself and your family
tomorrow: Sunday lunch: the women cook, the men sit. does Simran say it?

cards: Some questions sound like small talk and aren't. So, what does your family do? Which part of town?
What's your last name again? At dinner, Simran is telling the bus stop story, proud of Arjan for holding his head up, and Bebe asks, mildly, what his family's surname is. Simran answers.
Bebe nods, the way people nod when they've placed someone. Nobody says the word caste. Nobody has to.
Simran puts her fork down. So the question on the table is old: does the family you're born into rank you?

teach.h: SEE THE LIGHT, DON'T ASK THE CASTE.
teach.b: The Gurus answer no, plainly. Guru Nanak says on Ang 349, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; hereafter, there is no caste.

teach.h: THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE AS ONE.
teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh, in the Akal Ustat, puts it in one line: manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, recognize the whole human race as one. That's the line to tell a friend tonight: one human caste, in a Guru's own words.
And the langar puts it in your knees: everyone sits in one row, the pangat, and eats the same food. Honesty matters here too.

Caste names still linger in some Sikh families, in surnames, in marriage talk, in a nod at dinner. That's why today is about your own life, not someone else's. A neighbor tradition says something close.

teach.h: ACTS: OF ONE BLOOD ALL NATIONS.
teach.b: Paul, standing in Athens in the Book of Acts, tells the crowd that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.” Shared ground: one human family, no ranking by birth.
Paul grounds it in one blood, a common origin from one Maker. Guru Nanak grounds it in one light, shining now inside each person.
Simran asks Bebe, quietly, why the name mattered. Bebe is quiet for a long time. Then: it mattered in my village.
Let me think about your kitchen.

how: In the gurdwara's langar, everyone sits together in one row and eats the same food, whatever their background, and Sikh teaching rejects ranking people by caste.

games.q: what does “caste in your own life” mean?
o: keeping each family's traditions separate and proud
noticing ranking by birth in yourself, and refusing it
a rule about which jobs a family is allowed to do

p: see the light, don't ask the caste
the whole human race as one

s: Sikh teaching keeps caste, but asks people to be polite about it
Guru Nanak says don't ask about caste, and Guru Gobind Singh says recognize the whole human race as one.
Guru Gobind Singh wrote 'recognize the whole human race as one'
manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, in the Akal Ustat.

Acts 17:26 (KJV): 'hath made of one blood all nations of men.'

games.q: your uncle says your cousin's new partner is 'lovely, just not our kind of family.' going by today, what fits best?
o: ask him, kindly, what 'our kind' means, and say what you see in her.
agree with him, since families know best what works for them.
laugh it off; it's an old-school thing and it isn't your business.
games.why: Guru Nanak: recognize the light, don't ask about caste. noticing it in your own family, gently and out loud, is where today's lesson lives.

practice: Take a pen and write down one quick judgment you've caught yourself making about someone because of their family, their name, or where they're from. Under it, write: recognize the light.
Read both lines slowly, and leave the paper where you'll see it.

wordCard.voice: Caste in your own life. Noticing the quiet ranking by birth in yourself and your family, and choosing the light over the name.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jaat, caste or kind. Guru Gobind Singh: manas ki jaat, one human kind.

carryVoice: Carry this: no caste, one light, one human race. Bebe is still thinking, and that counts for day 1728.
